title: What are the three output modes in Structured Streaming — Append (only new rows), Complete (entire result table rewritten, for aggregations), Update (only changed rows) — and when do you use each?
shortTitle: The three output modes in Structured Streaming

s1_definition.profdef: Structured Streaming's output mode controls which rows of the result table are written to the sink on each trigger. Append mode emits only rows that are new and will never change again, which suits stateless transforms and aggregations finalized by a watermark. Complete mode rewrites the entire result table every trigger, which is only valid for aggregations and is used when the sink needs a full snapshot. Update mode emits only the rows whose values changed since the last trigger, which is the efficient middle ground for running aggregations where you want incremental changes rather than new-rows-only or a full rewrite.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India think of a dashboard showing totals per account. Append mode is like only ever posting brand-new, final entries that will never be revised — good for a raw transaction log. Complete mode is like reprinting the entire totals board from scratch every few seconds — correct but wasteful when the board is huge. Update mode is like a clerk who only rubs out and rewrites the few account totals that actually changed since last time — efficient and exactly what a live totals dashboard wants.
s1_definition.oneliner: Append writes only new final rows, Complete rewrites the whole result table each trigger (aggregations only), and Update writes only the rows that changed — pick Update for efficient running aggregations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Structured Streaming's output mode controls which rows of the result table are written to the sink on each trigger. Append mode emits only rows that are new and will never change again, which suits stateless transforms and aggregations finalized by a watermark. Complete mode rewrites the entire result table every trigger, which is only valid for aggregations and is used when the sink needs a full snapshot. Update mode emits only the rows whose values changed since the last trigger, which is the efficient middle ground for running aggregations where you want incremental changes rather than new-rows-only or a full rewrite.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India think of a dashboard showing totals per account. Append mode is like only ever posting brand-new, final entries that will never be revised — good for a raw transaction log. Complete mode is like reprinting the entire totals board from scratch every few seconds — correct but wasteful when the board is huge. Update mode is like a clerk who only rubs out and rewrites the few account totals that actually changed since last time — efficient and exactly what a live totals dashboard wants.

**One line to remember:** Append writes only new final rows, Complete rewrites the whole result table each trigger (aggregations only), and Update writes only the rows that changed — pick Update for efficient running aggregations.

sections.s2_technical:
Append mode writes only rows added to the result table that are guaranteed never to change again. For a stateless query like a filter or a map, every output row is final, so Append is the natural mode: `writeStream.outputMode("append")`. For aggregations, Append can still be used but only with a watermark, because Spark can only emit an aggregate once the watermark passes the window and guarantees no later update. Append is the only mode that works with file sinks, because files cannot be rewritten in place.

Complete mode rewrites the entire result table to the sink on every trigger. It is only valid for aggregation queries, because Spark must hold the full result in state to re-emit it. You use it when the sink needs a complete snapshot each time — for example writing a small per-account totals table to a key-value store or a dashboard that expects the full picture. The cost is that the whole result is written every trigger, so it does not scale to a result table with millions of groups.

Update mode writes only the rows whose value changed since the previous trigger. For a running `groupBy("accountId").count()`, if only three accounts received transactions in this micro-batch, only those three rows are emitted. This is the efficient choice for incremental aggregations going to an upsert-capable sink like a database or Kafka compacted topic, because you transmit the minimum necessary changes. Update is the default mental model for most streaming aggregations.

The choice is constrained by both the query and the sink. A file sink supports only Append. Aggregations without a watermark cannot use Append because Spark cannot know an aggregate is final. Complete requires an aggregation and a sink that can accept a full rewrite. Update requires a sink that can upsert by key. Getting the pairing wrong produces an analysis error at query start, so Spark fails fast rather than producing wrong output.

A senior-level nuance is that output mode interacts with state cleanup and watermarks. In Append mode with aggregation, the watermark both decides when a row becomes final and when its state can be dropped, so without a watermark the state grows unbounded and Append is rejected. In Complete mode state is never dropped because the full table must always be re-emittable, so Complete is only safe when the number of groups is bounded and small. Choosing the mode is therefore also a choice about memory and correctness, not just output volume.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India streams a raw, filtered transaction log to files for the audit team. Each row is final and files cannot be rewritten, so Append mode is the only correct choice.

Problem 2 — A small operations dashboard shows total transaction count for each of a handful of branch codes and expects the full board every refresh. Complete mode rewrites the entire small result table each trigger.

Problem 3 — A per-account running count feeds a database that upserts by account id, and only a few accounts change each micro-batch. Update mode emits only the changed account rows, which is the efficient choice.

The demo simulates one result table and shows what each output mode would emit for the same micro-batch, so the engineer can see Append emitting only new final rows, Complete emitting the whole table, and Update emitting only changed rows.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a result table of three account counts after one micro-batch. SAV2001 (3) and CUR3001 (2) changed this trigger; SAV9999 (7) did not change and is past the watermark, so it is finalized.

Step 1: Complete mode is applied. The emitter returns a copy of the entire result table — all three rows — because a Complete sink expects the full snapshot every trigger.

Step 2: Update mode is applied. The emitter filters to rows where changedThisTrigger is true, so only SAV2001 and CUR3001 are emitted. This is the minimal set of changes for an upsert sink.

Step 3: Append mode is applied. Only finalized rows that will never change again are eligible, which in this trigger is SAV9999. In real Spark the watermark decides finality; here it is pre-computed.

Step 4: The demo logs all three emissions side by side so the difference in volume and semantics is obvious.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:04:00 INFO    COMPLETE emits whole table: [SAV2001=3, CUR3001=2, SAV9999=7]
2026-10-30 05:04:00 INFO    UPDATE emits changed rows:  [SAV2001=3, CUR3001=2]
2026-10-30 05:04:00 INFO    APPEND emits finalized rows: [SAV9999=7]
2026-10-30 05:04:00 INFO    Output mode comparison complete.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Result table after micro-batch
  [SAV2001=3*  CUR3001=2*  SAV9999=7]   (* = changed this trigger)
    │
    ├─ COMPLETE ─→ rewrite ALL rows ───────→ [SAV2001=3, CUR3001=2, SAV9999=7]
    │              (aggregation only; small bounded table)
    │
    ├─ UPDATE ───→ only changed rows ──────→ [SAV2001=3, CUR3001=2]
    │              (upsert sink; efficient)
    │
    └─ APPEND ───→ only finalized rows ────→ [SAV9999=7]
                   (stateless, or watermarked agg; file sink)
```

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │        ResultRow         │  rows  │   OutputModeEmitter          │
  │ ──────────────────────── │───────▶│ ──────────────────────────   │
  │ - accountId: String      │        │ + complete(table): List     │
  │ - count: long            │        │ + update(table): List       │
  │ - changedThisTrigger: bool│       │ + append(finalized): List   │
  └──────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. main()
  2.   → emitter.complete(table)  → all 3 rows
  3.   → emitter.update(table)    → 2 changed rows

sections.s6_takeaway:
Structured Streaming has three output modes, and the output mode decides which rows of the result table get written to the sink on each trigger. Append mode writes only rows that are new and final and will never change again, which is the natural choice for stateless transforms and the only mode a file sink supports; for an aggregation you can use Append only with a watermark, because Spark needs to know an aggregate is final before it emits it. Complete mode rewrites the entire result table every trigger and is only valid for aggregations, so I use it when a sink needs a full snapshot and the number of groups is small and bounded. Update mode writes only the rows that changed since the last trigger, which is the efficient middle ground for running aggregations going to an upsert-capable sink.

The choice is constrained by both the query and the sink, and Spark fails fast at query start if the pairing is invalid. A file sink forces Append. An aggregation without a watermark cannot use Append. Complete needs an aggregation and a sink that accepts a full rewrite. Update needs a sink that can upsert by key. There is also a correctness and memory dimension: in Append with aggregation the watermark controls both finality and state cleanup, so without it state grows unbounded, and Complete never drops state because the whole table must stay re-emittable.

At the National Bank of India I used all three. A filtered raw transaction log streamed to S3 files in Append mode because each row is final and files cannot be rewritten. A small branch-level dashboard that wanted the whole totals board used Complete mode. And the main per-account running count fed a PostgreSQL table that upserts by account id, so it used Update mode and emitted only the handful of accounts that changed each micro-batch. In interviews I summarize it as: Append for new final rows and file sinks, Complete for small full-snapshot aggregations, and Update for efficient incremental aggregations to an upsert sink.

---

keyPoints: Structured Streaming: micro-batch or continuous processing
Watermark: handle late data — discard after threshold
Checkpoint: fault tolerance — recover state on failure
